$comment: THE SQLITE HARNESS LEG CATALOGUE — the declared, HOST-FREE answer to 'which targets does this harness build?'. D-HARNESS-CROSS-HOST-ANY-TARGET item (2). ★ THE RULE THIS FILE EXISTS TO ENFORCE: the set of legs is a property of the HARNESS, not of the machine running it. Read this file on Windows, on Linux, on an arm64 VPS or on a Mac and you get the SAME five legs. What the host changes is ONLY whether it can EXECUTE a leg's artifact — a separate question, answered by `runOn` + `launchers` below and never by an `if host == ...` in a driver. Before this file existed, build-and-test.sh derived its leg list from `uname` (pe64 was unreachable from any host, macho only from a Mac) and build-and-test.ps1 refused to start unless $IsWindows (pe64 was its ONLY leg, hardcoded). Each driver therefore conflated HOST with TARGET, which is the opposite of the user's hard requirement: 'build ANY target inside ANY host, this MUST work.'
$vocabularyComment: The declaration vocabulary is the CORPUS's, not a new one: `spec` and `runOn` mean exactly what they mean in examples/**/expected.json, and the verdicts a driver records for a leg come from the closed 7+1-name set in tests/test_support/arm_verdict_ledger.hpp (pinned by tests/harness/test_sqlite_harness_legs.cpp, which compares this catalogue's resolver output against that C++ enum). `launchers` is the ONE strict extension: the corpus's `emulator` key covers a cross-ARCH host on the SAME OS, and this harness additionally needs the cross-OS case (a pe64 artifact under Wine on Linux), so both are expressed as one ordered list of declared launchers keyed by (hostOs, hostArch). Absence of a matching launcher entry IS the 'none declared' declaration — there is no empty-string spelling, so a reader cannot mistake 'we looked and there is none' for 'nobody filled this in'. ★ EVERY launcher entry additionally declares `pathTranslation`: the PATH NAMESPACE its argv lives in, from the closed set in harness_legs.py (`none`, `windows-to-wsl`). It is required on every entry, never defaulted, for the same reason `zconfGuards` is: a reader must not have to know a default, and `none` — 'this launcher takes the driver's paths verbatim' — is a CLAIM about the launcher, not an absence. It exists because a launcher need not share a filesystem namespace with the driver that spawns it: `wine /home/me/x.exe` takes the driver's own path, `wsl.exe` needs `/mnt/c/...` where the driver holds a drive-letter path, and an untranslated path does not fail as a path error — the callee opens a relative file by that name, misses, and the run reads as a broken binary. The verb is resolved and APPLIED by harness_legs.py (`--translate-path` / `--assert-translated`), so the translator is named in one file and not in two drivers. ★★ AND `envTransfer`, THE SECOND HALF OF THE SAME FACT, found by measuring the first: a launcher in another OS namespace does not inherit the driver's ENVIRONMENT either. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-04 — a `wsl.exe`-launched fixture saw `SQLITE_TEST_PATTERN_LIST` and `QUICKTEST_OMIT` as EMPTY, so the corpus RESUME ENGINE (which selects its files through that variable) silently re-ran the corpus from the beginning instead of from the abort point: a harness that looks like it is working and is not. `inherit` = the child gets this driver's environment block (qemu, Wine, `arch`); `wslenv` = each variable must be NAMED in the `WSLENV` carrier. Resolved by harness_legs.py (`--env-transfer`), so the carrier and its separator are spelled once. ★★★ AND THE THIRD NAMESPACE, `runFilesystem`, FOUND THE SAME WAY THE SECOND WAS — BY MEASURING THE FIRST TWO AND FINDING THEM INSUFFICIENT [[D-HARNESS-WSL-LAUNCHED-LEG-RUNDIR-IS-DRVFS]]. `pathTranslation` says how a launcher SPELLS a path; `envTransfer` says whether it sees this driver's environment; NEITHER says which FILESYSTEM the launched process writes its databases onto — and the subject of this corpus is a database engine, so that is the one property it tests hardest. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-06 on this host, one process, two directories: `/mnt/c/…` (`9p … aname=drvfs`, **no `metadata` option**) answers `chmod 644` with **777** and `chmod 400` with **555**, because DrvFs derives the entire POSIX mode from the single Windows read-only ATTRIBUTE; `/tmp` (ext4) answers 644 and 400. ✔AND MEASURED BY A 2x2 MATCHED CONTROL ({DSS fixture, gcc reference} x {DrvFs rundir, ext4 rundir}, same staged corpus): **all 60 failures reproduce IDENTICALLY under the GCC REFERENCE on DrvFs and VANISH on ext4** — wal2 20, zipfile 12, e_walauto 10, journal3 8, attach 2, tkt3457 1, plus a `pager4` ABORT — i.e. ZERO of them are DSS-attributable. `driver` = the launched process writes where this driver writes (Wine's Z: mapping, qemu, `arch` — all one machine, one kernel, one filesystem); `wsl-linux` = the launcher crosses into a Linux kernel whose own filesystem is ext4 and which reaches this driver's files only through that compatibility mount. Required on EVERY entry, never defaulted, because `driver` is a CLAIM and it was the unexamined one. Resolved by harness_legs.py (`--run-dir-plan`), which also splices the launcher's working-directory option and hands back the argv prefixes that create/clear/populate the directory — so neither driver spells `--cd`, `mkdir`, `rm -rf` or `cp` for a foreign filesystem, and neither knows where in an argv an option has to go. ⛔ THE 60 FAILURES ARE NOT CONFOUNDS AND MUST NEVER BECOME ONE: the mechanism is ours and it is fixable, so a `confounds` row for them would launder a harness misconfiguration into 'expected' using the very mechanism that key exists to keep honest.
$confoundsComment: ★★ AN EARNED CONFOUND IS A PROPERTY OF THE LEG, NOT OF THE DRIVER YOU HAPPENED TO RUN [[D-HARNESS-CONFOUND-LEDGER-IS-PER-DRIVER-NOT-PER-LEG]], [[D-HARNESS-SQLITE-CONFOUNDS-NOT-DECLARED-PER-LEG]], [[D-SQLITE-CONFOUND-LIST-DRIVER-ASYMMETRY]]. A confound is a unit failure this harness has PROVEN is not the compiler's, by a matched control, on a named leg, on a named date — and since the count of GENUINE failures is what every verdict rests on, which failures are excused decides what this project believes about itself. Until this key existed the answer depended on WHICH DRIVER YOU RAN: `build-and-test.sh` read one global `DSS_CONFOUNDS` and applied it to EVERY leg including legs where nothing had ever been measured, while `build-and-test.ps1` returned an earned list for `pe64-x86_64` and an EMPTY one for everything else — and all six of its patterns had been earned on LINUX x86_64, so the Windows driver handed a Linux-earned list to the one leg that could not use it and withheld it from the legs that had earned it. ✔MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: the same elf64-x86_64 artefact's `zipfile-25.0` was a 'known non-DSS confound' under one driver and a 'genuine failure' under the other, in the same project on the same day, so no two legs' genuine-failure counts were comparable. ⇒ the declaration lives HERE, per leg, and every pattern carries `earnedOn` / `earnedAt` / `mechanism` / `anchor`; the lint REFUSES a pattern that does not show its work, refuses a duplicate, refuses one that does not compile as a regex, and refuses a missing key — because `[]` (nothing has ever been earned on this leg, every failure counts) is a CLAIM a catalogue has to make out loud, and a missing key could not be told from it. ★★★ AND SINCE 2026-08-11, `requires` — THE CONDITION, MACHINE-READABLE [[D-HARNESS-CONFOUND-SCOPE-IS-A-RUN-MODE-NOT-A-HOST]]. Read `$environmentProbesComment` for the mechanism. ⓘ WHAT THE OLD SHAPE ENFORCED WAS STRICTLY LESS THAN THIS PARAGRAPH CLAIMS, and the gap is worth naming because the sentence above is the project's own standard: a confound is 'a unit failure this harness has PROVEN is not the compiler's, BY A MATCHED CONTROL, on a named leg, on a named date' — but `scope: any` plus a prose `earnedOn` enforced only 'somebody wrote a sentence here'. Where the mechanism is a property of the MACHINE, `any` actively contradicted the definition: it excused the family on machines the control was never run on and could not have been. `requires` closes that gap for the mechanisms this harness can measure. ⚠ `scope` IS NOW LEGACY, NOT AN ALTERNATIVE: `scope: any` is REFUSED (that claim is `requires: []`), and a row may stay on `native`/`emulated` only while it NAMES what stops it migrating (`scopeLegacyBlocker`, enforced by the lint). The axis retires when the last row leaves it — deleted, the way `copy-relocation` was, never left inert for the next row to reach for. ⛔ AND `scope: emulated` WAS REJECTED AS THE FIX FOR THE CLOCK ROWS, on the record: it is a PROXY, [[D-TEST-PE64-CONFOUND-PIN-WEAKENED-BY-ITS-OWN-SUBJECT]] records this same pin re-cut TWICE by the very cases it was meant to judge, and it is provably wrong in BOTH directions — it would excuse walsetlk under Wine on a healthy-clock box, and the `^writecrash-` row below already documents the proxy breaking the other way on an arm64 Windows host. A proxy with two recorded failures is not a candidate. ⚠ THE OPERATOR OVERRIDE (`DSS_CONFOUNDS`) IS UNCHANGED AND STILL APPLIES TO EVERY LEG: an operator naming a pattern is stating intent for this run, not inheriting one, and both drivers announce which of the two is in force.
$noHostKeyingComment: NOTHING in this file may be keyed on the host. `build.libraries.searchPaths` is the one place host-shaped STRINGS appear, and they are CANDIDATES, not decisions: every path is tried on every host, a hit is used and a miss costs nothing. A driver that skips a search path because of the host it is on has reintroduced the defect. ⚠ If you are tempted to add a `"onlyOnHost"` key here, stop: the question you are answering is either 'can this host EXECUTE it' (that is `runOn`/`launchers`) or 'is a declared build input present' (that is a filesystem probe whose failure is the LOUD `skipped-build-input-missing` verdict) — never 'is this leg allowed to exist'. ★★★ AND THE RULE STATED POSITIVELY, BECAUSE THE THREE ADMISSIBLE QUESTIONS ABOVE ARE AN ENUMERATION AND AN ENUMERATION INVITES A FOURTH ENTRY BY STEALTH (added 2026-08-11, [[D-HARNESS-CONFOUND-SCOPE-IS-A-RUN-MODE-NOT-A-HOST]]): **A MEASURED PROPERTY OF THE RUNNING ENVIRONMENT IS ADMISSIBLE; A NAME FOR THE ENVIRONMENT NEVER IS.** That is what every one of the three already is — `runOn` is a declared capability, `launchers` is keyed on (hostOs, hostArch) as the ADDRESS of a measurement and never as permission, and the build-input gate is a FILESYSTEM PROBE. `environmentProbes` below is the fourth instance of the SAME rule and not an exception to it: `clock-realtime-steps` answers 'does the clock on the machine I am running on jump', by watching it, and its answer is checkable, publishable and FALSE on a healthy box. `if host == 'wsl'` remains forbidden for the reason that has always applied — a name is not evidence, it cannot be wrong out loud, and it is stale the day the machine is replaced.
$environmentProbesComment: ★★★ THE CONDITION UNDER WHICH AN EXCUSE HOLDS, MOVED OUT OF PROSE AND INTO A MEASUREMENT [[D-HARNESS-CONFOUND-SCOPE-IS-A-RUN-MODE-NOT-A-HOST]]. ⓘ THE DEFECT, IN ONE CLAUSE, AND THIS FILE ALREADY KNEW IT: legs[1]'s `$confoundsComment` said the clock rows are declared because the mechanism is 'a property of the HOST'S CLOCK, which both Linux legs share WHEN THIS HARNESS IS DRIVEN FROM THIS BOX.' The condition was ALREADY STATED — in prose, because the schema had no field for it — so `^walsetlk-` sat at `scope: any` on both ELF legs and would have silently excused a GENUINE walsetlk failure on the arm64 VPS, where the clock has never been shown to step. That is exactly the `earnedOn` failure one field along: a load-bearing condition recorded where nothing reads it. ⇒ a confound row may declare `requires: [<probe name>]`, and it is honoured ONLY where the named probe MEASURES its defect as PRESENT. `requires: []` is the unconditional claim and is the common answer. ★ THE ENGINE HAS NO PROBE-NAME BRANCH: each entry names a `verb` from the closed table in harness_legs.py (`ENVIRONMENT_PROBE_VERBS`), and the engine dispatches on the verb. A second clock probe needs NO code; a new KIND of measurement adds a verb, which is a vocabulary extension exactly like `runFilesystem` or `envTransfer`. ★★★ AND SINCE 2026-08-12 THE MEASUREMENT IS TAKEN IN THE KERNEL THE FIXTURE RUNS IN, NOT IN THE DRIVER'S [[D-HARNESS-ENVIRONMENT-PROBE-MEASURES-THE-DRIVERS-KERNEL-NOT-THE-LAUNCHED-ONE]]. A probe answers a question about a MACHINE, and a leg launched through `wsl.exe` executes on a different one from the driver that planned it — so the verdicts are keyed on the KERNEL and a leg reads the drawer for its own. The entry mechanism is DECLARED per `runFilesystem` in harness_legs.py (`kernelEntryArgv` / `kernelProbeInterpreter` / `kernelEntryPathTranslation`), in the same closed-table style as `sharesDriverKernel`, and the engine has no host branch and no launcher-name branch. ⚠ IT IS THE KERNEL BOUNDARY AND DELIBERATELY NOT THE LEG'S LAUNCHER: elf64-arm64 from Windows launches `wsl.exe -e qemu-aarch64`, and qemu-user is INSIDE the kernel `wsl.exe -e` already entered — it changes the instruction set, not the clock — so entering via `wsl.exe -e` is both sufficient and correct, and going through the full launcher argv would demand an aarch64 python3 that does not exist in order to measure something qemu cannot affect. ⇒ ONE SAMPLE PER DISTINCT KERNEL, reused by every leg that executes in it: ✔MEASURED 2026-08-12, a Windows `--plan` took 20.8 s total and measured `wsl-linux` ONCE for BOTH ELF legs while never sampling the Windows clock at all (every row on the legs that execute there is unconditional). ⛔ AND IF THAT KERNEL CANNOT BE ASKED — no interpreter in the distro, the entry mechanism fails, the answer is not a verdict map — the outcome is `unreachable`, every verdict for it is INDETERMINATE, the rows are INACTIVE and the report says so. FAIL TOWARD REPORTING: never `absent` (which reads as a clean bill) and never `present`. ★★ THE ERRORS ARE NOT SYMMETRIC AND EVERY PROBE IS BIASED TOWARD ABSENT. A FALSE NEGATIVE (absent on a defective box) un-excuses environment failures → noisy reds → somebody investigates and finds the clock: NOISY BUT SAFE. A FALSE POSITIVE (present on a healthy box) SILENTLY EXCUSES A REAL DSS MISCOMPILE: SILENT AND DANGEROUS, and it is the exact failure this mechanism exists to remove. So INDETERMINATE is honoured as ABSENT, both thresholds must be CLEARED rather than approached, and `config` may only ever TIGHTEN — harness_legs.py's lint refuses a value below the verb's floor, naming the asymmetry. ★ WHY THE THRESHOLDS ARE HERE AND THE FLOORS ARE IN CODE: tightening a probe must be an edit to this file, not a code change; but a threshold config can LOOSEN without limit is a guard that gets re-cut to fit whatever case is in front of it, which this project has already paid for twice ([[D-TEST-PE64-CONFOUND-PIN-WEAKENED-BY-ITS-OWN-SUBJECT]]). ⛔ NOT A CONFORMANCE QUESTION, AND IT MUST NOT BE DRESSED AS ONE: a stepping CLOCK_REALTIME violates nothing in C23 — §7.29 `timespec_get(…, TIME_UTC)` is explicitly WALL CLOCK and may jump, and C23 requires no monotonicity anywhere (that is POSIX `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, which these tests do not use). Manufacturing a conformance angle would weaken the row. The compatibility instrument that IS load-bearing here is the matched gcc reference. ★★ AND THE PROBE IS ONLY HALF THE ORACLE, deliberately: a PROBE answers 'may this family be honoured on this machine at all' (deterministic, per host, cheap); a REFERENCE-COMPILER CONTROL answers 'is THIS failure DSS-attributable' (per test, and for a timing test STOCHASTIC — gcc can pass while DSS fails on one run by luck, which is precisely what legs[0]'s `^walsetlk-` row records: different members, same family, same run). Neither replaces the other. A single green oracle run must not retire a probe, and a green probe must not stand in for the oracle.

clock-realtime-steps.measures: whether this machine's CLOCK_REALTIME jumps relative to its MONOTONIC clock — the wall clock moving when real elapsed time did not
clock-realtime-steps.presentMeans: every wall-clock assertion in the corpus that straddles a jump mismeasures its interval by the step magnitude, in either direction, with no involvement from the compiler under test. The instrument is the DIFFERENCE of two clocks on purpose: a descheduled process, a loaded box or a slow filesystem inflate BOTH deltas equally and cancel, so what survives is a jump and nothing else.
clock-realtime-steps.$calibrationComment: ✔THE MEASURED SIGNATURE this config is calibrated against (2026-08-01, TWO independent instruments): CLOCK_REALTIME oscillates between two values ~34.47 s apart, flipping every ~5 s; 49 and 48 steps observed; total spread 35.164 s. So a 20 s window at 250 ms sees ~4 flips — comfortably the two steps required, never a single pair of readings — and `minStepSeconds: 5` sits ~7x BELOW the real magnitude and ~4 orders of magnitude ABOVE scheduler noise. Both gaps are deliberate: the first so a partially-degraded clock is still caught, the second so nothing but a jump can clear it.

$configureAnswersComment: ★★ AND THE SAME STORY ONE LAYER UP, FOR SQLITE'S OWN `./configure` (D-HARNESS-MACHO-LEG-INHERITS-THE-DERIVING-LINUX-HOSTS-CONFIGURE-PROBES). The recipe is derived by running `make -n` on the DERIVING host, and the ONE host-probe define left on that command line is `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H` — which makes `sqliteInt.h` `#include "sqlite_cfg.h"`, and the include path points at the deriving host's build dir. So EVERY leg inherited THAT machine's ~52 configure answers wholesale. ✔MEASURED, the whole chain, on the macho64-arm64 CLI: the Linux `sqlite_cfg.h` sets `HAVE_PREAD64`/`HAVE_PWRITE64` → `os_unix.c` `#if defined(HAVE_PREAD64) && defined(HAVE_PWRITE64)` → `USE_PREAD64` → the `osPread64`/`osPwrite64` macros, typed with **`off64_t`** — a type Darwin does not have. `off64_t` + `pread64` + `pwrite64` are ONE defect, not three. ⛔ There is NO `HAVE_OFF64_T` macro anywhere in sqlite; the pe64 leg's `$recipeTransformComment` used to name one, and it never existed — that prose is corrected below. ★ THE CLASS IS CLOSED BY MACHINE DIFF, not by reasoning about the header: the deriving Linux `sqlite_cfg.h` against the Mac's OWN configure-generated one differ on EXACTLY THREE LINES — `HAVE_PREAD64`, `HAVE_PWRITE64`, `HAVE_MALLOC_H` — and all ~49 other answers (`HAVE_FDATASYNC`, `HAVE_GMTIME_R`, `HAVE_LOCALTIME_R`, `HAVE_USLEEP`, `HAVE_UTIME`, `HAVE_ISNAN`, `HAVE_NANOSLEEP`, `HAVE_REALPATH`, `HAVE_DLOPEN`, `HAVE_ZLIB`, the `HAVE_INT*_T` family, `SIZEOF_OFF_T 8`, …) are BYTE-IDENTICAL. That is why each leg declares THREE answers and not fifty: it declares only what `configure` actually VARIES across the targets this harness builds, and the deriving host answers the rest — correctly, because on those rows the two machines agree. Each leg's `build.configureAnswers` is REQUIRED, its values are real JSON booleans, and harness_legs.py's lint CROSS-CHECKS every one against the leg's own target (a Darwin leg declaring `HAVE_PREAD64: true` is refused, naming the evidence), so a wrong declaration fails the lint instead of shipping. The drivers then stage ONE `sqlite_cfg.h` per TARGET OS — the deriving host's answers for the identical rows, the leg's declared answers for the three that vary — into the harness's OWN cfg/ dir, placed AHEAD of the deriving host's build dir on the include list. `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H` STAYS. ⚠ NOTE THE KEY IS THE TARGET OS AND NOT THE `recipeTransform`: four legs share `"none"` and they are TWO configurations (two Linux, two Darwin), so keying this on the transform would hand Darwin the Linux answers again — which is the defect. ⛔ TWO ALTERNATIVES WERE REJECTED, recorded because both are the obvious thing to reach for. (1) DERIVE THE RECIPE PER TARGET, on a machine of that target: that is what upstream's build system expects and it is why a native build never has this bug, but it makes the Darwin legs unbuildable on the four hosts out of five that are not a Mac — flatly the host-lock this file exists to end. (2) A BLUNT `darwin-selfconfig` TRANSFORM that just drops `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H`, mirroring `windows-selfconfig`: ✔MEASURED to WORK, and still wrong — it discards ~49 CORRECT answers to fix 3 wrong ones, ~10 of them with real consequences (`HAVE_GMTIME_R`/`HAVE_LOCALTIME_R` fall back to the NON-REENTRANT `gmtime`/`localtime` in a SQLITE_THREADSAFE=1 build; `HAVE_FDATASYNC` becomes `#define fdatasync fsync`; `HAVE_USLEEP` drops sqlite3_sleep to 1-SECOND granularity, which the timing-sensitive corpus WILL notice). The same blunt drop is acceptable on WINDOWS only because `SQLITE_OS_WIN` re-configures the whole `os_win.c` path and none of those Unix answers is consulted there.
$stagedHeadersComment: ★ THE THIRD-PARTY HEADERS A LEG COMPILES AGAINST ARE A TARGET FACT, NOT A HOST ONE (D-HARNESS-SQLITE-STAGE-ZCONF-IS-PE-SHAPED, closed TF-C115). The staged zlib header is copied from the DERIVING POSIX host, where `./configure` baked ITS OWN probe results into zconf.h — `#if 1 → #define Z_HAVE_UNISTD_H` and friends. Those are facts about the deriving machine, exactly like the recipe's HAVE_*/Z_HAVE_* defines that `recipeTransform` exists to drop, and handing them to a foreign target is the same cross-compile category error one level down. Each leg therefore DECLARES `build.zconfGuards` — the value ITS target has for each guard `./configure` may have set — and the drivers stage ONE zinc/ PER `recipeTransform` (stage-zinc.py, called by both) and give each leg an include list pointing at its own. Two legs may share a zinc/ only by sharing a recipeTransform, and the lint refuses a catalogue where same-transform legs declare different guards. Before this, ONE pe-shaped zinc/ served every leg and the .ps1 REFUSED (`poisoned`) any leg that was not `windows-selfconfig` rather than compile it against the wrong header — the right call, and the reason this key exists is to make the refusal unnecessary instead of relaxing it.
$loadExtHelperBuilderComment: ★★★ THE COMPILER THIS REPOSITORY SHIPS BUILDS THE CORPUS'S dlopen()ed HELPER — NO HOST NEEDS A THIRD-PARTY CROSS-COMPILER FOR ANY LEG. Operator, 2026-08-05: 'why do we need mingw? since dss code prime should not have dependencies?' / 'I installed mingw in wsl, but we should NOT depend on a tool'. The `$targetCcComment` below is still TRUE and its rule is unchanged — a compiler's name is not a declaration of its target — but the SHAPE it left behind made every leg's RUN conditional on this machine owning a cross-compiler for that leg's target (a mingw gcc for pe64, aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc for the arm64 leg, an Apple clang for the two macho legs), and a leg without one recorded `skipped-build-input-missing` and did not run its ~330,000 units. That is the same host-lock D-HARNESS-CROSS-HOST-ANY-TARGET exists to end, one layer down from the fixture. ⇒ each leg now DECLARES `build.sharedLibFormat` and DSS emits the helper for it. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-05 on this project's WINDOWS box — one host, all five legs, rc=0 and zero diagnostics on every one: pe64 8,704 B · elf64-x86_64 13,912 B · elf64-aarch64 13,912 B · macho64-arm64 67,426 B · macho64-x86_64 17,890 B. The three a machine here can LOAD were loaded THROUGH SQLITE'S OWN `sqlite3_load_extension()` (dlopen + dlsym `testloadext_init`, exactly what test/loadext.test does) and `SELECT half(9.0)` returned 4.500 — pe64 natively on Windows, elf64-x86_64 in WSL, elf64-aarch64 under qemu-aarch64; the loading program was built by the REFERENCE compiler each time, so the only thing under test was the DSS artefact. ★ THE CONTROL IS KEPT, DELIBERATELY, BECAUSE DSS IS NOW TESTING DSS: a defect SHARED by the fixture and the helper (both compile sqlite3ext.h) could cancel and read as green. So wherever a VERIFIED target compiler happens to exist, the same source is ALSO built with it and both artefacts are reported side by side — never gating, never staging — and `DSS_LOADEXT_HELPER=reference` STAGES the control instead, which makes the corpus itself the differential. There is NO automatic fallback: a DSS emission failure is a compiler defect and this harness exists to surface them, so it is `poisoned` with the diagnostics quoted, never quietly rebuilt another way.
$targetCcComment: ★★ A COMPILER'S NAME IS NOT A DECLARATION OF ITS TARGET, and this catalogue once said it was. ⚠ READ `$loadExtHelperBuilderComment` FIRST: since 2026-08-05 this key governs the optional CONTROL arm, not a required build input — a leg whose `targetCc` resolves to nothing on this host still builds its helper (with DSS) and still runs its corpus. D-HARNESS-LOADEXT-HELPER-TARGET-BLINDNESS-NOW-ABORTS-THE-RUN. `build.targetCc.candidates` is a list of names to TRY, in order; it is NOT a list of compilers that are known to build this leg. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-05 on a WSL/Ubuntu x86_64 host: both elf legs ran GREEN (6 err / 331,351 and 5 err / 331,355, all known confounds) and the run then DIED in /usr/bin/ld — 'relocation R_X86_64_PC32 against symbol `sqlite3_api` can not be used when making a shared object; recompile with -fPIC' — building the pe64 leg's loadext helper, and pe64's units never ran. The mingw cross-compiler was absent, this leg listed plain `gcc` as an ALTERNATIVE, and so a LINUX compiler was picked, legitimately, to build a WINDOWS shared object. build-and-test.sh:2615 and :3804 both forbid exactly that fallback in so many words; neither guard fired, because the config had already licensed what the guards were watching for. ⇒ THE RESOLVER NOW ASKS THE COMPILER. harness_legs.py `--resolve-target-cc <leg>` accepts a candidate only if `<cc> -dumpmachine` names this leg's own target arch AND target OS, both derived from the leg's declared `spec`. No new key, because the leg already declares its target; no host test; no format-name branch. A candidate that CANNOT state its target (the probe fails) is REFUSED, never assumed — the leg is still BUILT, it records `skipped-build-input-missing`, and its corpus does not run. ★ AND THE RULE IS NOT pe64-SHAPED: the elf64-x86_64 leg's `cc`/`gcc`/`clang` resolve to an aarch64 compiler on this project's native arm64 Linux VPS, which is the wrong-arch helper D-HARNESS-ARM64-LEG-HOST-ARCH-HELPER-SO is named after; the same one check refuses it. ★★ WHAT IT BUILDS is the corpus's dlopen()ed helper extension, whose FILE NAME is also a target fact — see each leg's `loadExtHelperName`.
$referenceOracleComment: ★★★ THE ATTRIBUTION ORACLE IS A PER-LEG FACT, AND `targetCc` IS ITS DECLARATION TOO — ONE list of "compilers that PROVE they target this leg", read by TWO consumers (the loadext control arm above, and the same-platform reference oracle). A second candidate list would have been a second thing to keep in step, and the question both consumers ask is identical. D-HARNESS-PE64-HAS-NO-SAME-PLATFORM-ORACLE: the harness builds ONE reference testfixture per run with the DERIVING host's gcc, so it is an ELF Linux binary, and Step 9 printed a single `oracle` line for the whole run — which for pe64 and the two mach-o legs NAMED A BINARY OF ANOTHER PLATFORM and READ AS AN AVAILABLE CONTROL. The verdict is now derived per leg from two MEASURED inputs (the reference binary's own target, read out of its header by --identify-binary, against this leg's declared `spec`) and a leg with no same-platform reference reports NO ORACLE in those terms, plus the weaker fallback control by name. `--build-reference-oracle` then compiles the leg's OWN .dss-project.json manifest — the same sources/includes/defines/resolveLibraries dss consumed — with the verified compiler, which is the only shape that CAN work cross-target: upstream's autotools Makefile is configured for the deriving host and cannot emit a foreign-target fixture. `build.referenceLinkFlags` is the one thing the manifest does not carry: the TARGET's system libraries the reference link needs (POSIX targets want -lm/-ldl/-lpthread; a Windows target wants none, mingw links its own). It is not a plain command entry: wsl.exe lives in a DIFFERENT PATH NAMESPACE from the driver that spawns it (`pathTranslation`) AND in a different ENVIRONMENT namespace (`envTransfer`). The second was found by measuring the first — with paths translated but the environment assumed to inherit, the corpus resume engine's file selection arrived EMPTY and the resume re-ran the whole corpus while looking like it worked. ★★★ AND THE THIRD NAMESPACE, WHICH IS THE ARGV ITSELF: the command is `wsl.exe -e`, and this entry said `wsl.exe --` until 2026-08-04. `--` is documented as 'pass the remaining command line as is' and it is NOT the same as `-e`/`--exec` — ✔MEASURED on this host, one variable changed: `wsl.exe -- /nope` answers `/bin/bash: line 1: /nope: No such file` while `wsl.exe -e /nope` answers `execvpe(/nope) failed`, i.e. `--` reconstructs a command LINE and feeds it to the distro's DEFAULT SHELL. build.$recipeTransformComment: The recipe is derived from a POSIX `make -n`, so any host feature-probe define it carries is a fact about the DERIVING host, never about this target. `windows-selfconfig` drops those and adds SQLITE_OS_WIN=1 so SQLite self-configures its Windows build. ⚠ WHICH DEFINES, PRECISELY — ✔MEASURED 2026-08-05 (TF-C121) against the recipe this harness actually derives: `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H` is the ONE such define on the command line. There is NO bare `HAVE_*` and NO `Z_HAVE_*` in `stage/defines.txt` or `stage/cli-defines.txt` at all (the only near-miss is `SQLITE_HAVE_ZLIB=1`, a project feature flag the transform's `^(HAVE_|Z_HAVE_)` regex deliberately does not match). This comment used to list `HAVE_*/Z_HAVE_*` alongside it as if all three families were present; the regex arm is a standing guard against a future recipe, not a description of this one. See `$configureAnswersComment` above, which states the same fact, and gen-pe64-manifest.py's transform block. Keyed on THIS LEG, which is why the rule moved out of gen-pe64-manifest.py's prose ('this generator is pe-only, so keying the rule on the pe target is inherent here') into a declaration any driver can read.
build.$zconfGuardsComment: THE HEADER HALF OF THE SAME CROSS-COMPILE CATEGORY ERROR the recipeTransform fixes, and until TF-C115 the ONLY leg it was applied for — by a `perl -0777 -pi` flip buried in one driver's staging step, against ONE zinc/ shared by every leg, which is why a non-pe leg had to be REFUSED (`poisoned`) rather than built. The staged zconf.h comes from the deriving POSIX host, where ./configure wrote `#if 1 → #define Z_HAVE_UNISTD_H`; that is a fact about THAT HOST, and on a Windows TARGET <unistd.h> does not exist. Each guard is now DECLARED per leg and one zinc/ is staged per recipeTransform (stage-zinc.py), so every leg parses a zlib header configured for ITS OWN target and no leg is refused. ★ Z_HAVE_STDARG_H stays true: <stdarg.h> is C-standard and exists on pe. ★ MEASURED (TF-C115) on the elf64-x86_64 leg, both gcc and DSS: with these recipe defines the ONLY thing the guard changes is `z_off_t` = off_t vs long — the same 8-byte `long` on LP64 — and SEEK_*/z_off64_t/the gz* symbol names are byte-identical either way. So the flip is BENIGN on LP64; it is NOT benign on the pe target, where the guard's `#include <unistd.h>` simply does not resolve.
build.$configureAnswersComment: ★ DECLARED, AND INERT ON THIS LEG — both halves matter. INERT: `windows-selfconfig` drops `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H`, so sqliteInt.h never includes ANY sqlite_cfg.h here and no answer below is read. DECLARED ANYWAY: every leg declares every answer so a reader never has to know a default, and — more to the point — these are claims about the TARGET, which stay true whatever a transform does with them. `pread64`/`pwrite64` are glibc LFS64 names that no Windows CRT has. `HAVE_MALLOC_H` is TRUE: ✔MEASURED on this project's Windows box, the UCRT ships `malloc.h` under the Windows SDK's `ucrt/` include dir (`C:/Program Files (x86)/Windows Kits/10/Include/<ver>/ucrt/malloc.h`), so declaring it false would be a false statement about the target that happens to be unread. If this leg ever stops dropping `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H`, these are already the right answers and nothing here needs revisiting.

build.$librariesComment: pe64 --resolve-library reads a DLL's EXPORT table (.edata), so these must be real DLLs, not import .libs. A DLL is just a FILE: DSS reads a PE export table on any host, so ANY box that HAS these files can build this leg — and the old `search-paths` provider is precisely the reason no non-Windows box had them. ✔MEASURED: the leg was `skipped-build-input-missing` on the arm64 VPS and on macOS, because every declared search path was a Windows install location plus a cache nothing ever populated. Searching for a file the machine was never given is not acquisition. ⚠ THE OBVIOUS SOURCE IS BLOCKED, MEASURED 2026-08-06: msys2/mingw64 — the repo D-HARNESS-LIBRARY-ACQUISITION-BUILT-FOR-ONE-LEG-IN-ONE-DRIVER names, and the source of the very `tcl86.dll` Git for Windows ships — publishes `.pkg.tar.zst` and NOTHING ELSE (every tcl and zlib package, checked directly). zstd entered the Python stdlib in 3.14 and this project has a 3.12 host, so that route would be a capability that exists on one host and not another. conda-forge's win-64 packages are plain `.tar.bz2`, unauthenticated HTTPS, content-addressable, and carry the SCRIPT LIBRARY as well — so the pe64 leg becomes self-contained instead of borrowing from an installed Git.

libraries.$importNameComment: Bare DLL names, and on Windows that IS the beside-the-artefact spelling: the loader searches the application's own directory FIRST, so a DLL staged next to the executable wins with no path recorded and no assumption about the target's layout — the same argument `@loader_path` makes on Darwin, spelled the way this loader spells it. Each DLL's own PE export-directory Name already agrees (`tcl86t.dll`, `zlib.dll`), so nothing is being displaced here; it is declared because 'the packager's identity happens to be right' is a fact a reader should be able to check.
libraries.$tclNamesComment: `tcl86t.dll` is conda-forge's THREADED build — the `t` suffix is the Windows convention for `--enable-threads`, which is also how msys2 and ActiveState ship it, and what sqlite's testfixture wants. The older unsuffixed names stay in the list: they are what a `search-paths` era cache or a Git-for-Windows install still holds, and this list is matched against whatever is staged.

archives.$archiveComment: conda-forge's `tk` package carries BOTH tcl86t.dll and tk86t.dll plus the whole `Library/lib/tcl8.6` script tree (830 files, ✔MEASURED, including init.tcl and Tcl's own tzdata). There is no separate `tcl` package for win-64 — Tcl ships inside `tk` — which is why the archive's name does not say Tcl.

The scripts are ARCHITECTURE-INDEPENDENT `.tcl` text, so this leg stages the SAME tree from the SAME pinned archive — into its OWN cache directory, because a leg's staged inputs are that leg's, and a shared directory would make 'which leg staged this?' unanswerable. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-06: the two slices' embedded path sets are IDENTICAL (14 tokens each), which is why the declaration below is identical too.

embeddedPaths.$why: MacPorts' libdir, reported through `tcl_pkgPath`/`tcl_library` for a package search that this fixture never performs — the testfixture loads no Tcl EXTENSION (its own commands are compiled in), and the one directory `tclInit` MUST read is declared runtime-data above.
TCL_PREFIX/bin, reported through `tcl_platform`/`info nameofexecutable` fallbacks. Nothing in the corpus execs out of it.
TCL_INCLUDE_SPEC, a BUILD-time answer baked in for tclConfig.sh consumers. This harness stages its own tcl.h (see the top-level Tcl coherence check) and never reads it.
the manual page directory, from the same tclConfig.sh block. No code path in a Tcl interpreter reads it.
the default PATH element Tcl's `exec` falls back on. A TARGET path that exists on every Mac, not a packager path — nothing to stage.
`exec`'s redirection sink. A device on the target, not data we could ship.
the controlling terminal, opened by `tcl_interactive` prompting. Same category as /dev/null.
the fallback temp directory for `file tempfile` when TMPDIR is unset. A target location, not shipped data.
the HFS+ resource-fork suffix Tcl appends when opening a file's resource fork; a magic SUFFIX, not a directory anyone stages.
